reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Caused by autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutations in FGFR1 or, more often and more severely, FGFR2
Craniosynostosis with midface hypoplasia and proptosis is combined with characteristically broad, medially deviated thumbs and great toes
Partial soft-tissue syndactyly of the hands and feet is common but is milder than the fusion seen in Apert syndrome
Type 1 (classic) has a good prognosis with usually normal intelligence, whereas types 2 and 3 are severe with major neurological risk
Type 2 shows a cloverleaf skull (kleeblattschadel) from multisuture fusion with extreme proptosis, while type 3 has a very short cranial base without the cloverleaf shape
Airway obstruction, tracheal cartilage anomalies and severe proptosis threatening the globe are important early hazards in the severe forms
Hydrocephalus, Chiari-type hindbrain herniation and raised intracranial pressure require neuroimaging surveillance
Management is by a craniofacial team with staged vault expansion, midface advancement and airway support
reference.pathophysiology: Pfeiffer syndrome is driven by activating mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 or 2 that amplify FGF signalling in cranial sutures and limb buds. Excess receptor activity promotes premature suture ossification and disturbs the development of the digits, producing broad, deviated thumbs and great toes with variable soft-tissue syndactyly. The degree of receptor activation broadly tracks with clinical severity, so the more disruptive FGFR2 changes tend to cause the multisuture, cloverleaf-skull phenotypes with greater neurological compromise.
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing of FGFR1 and FGFR2 to confirm diagnosis and subtype
Three-dimensional cranial CT to characterise suture fusion and detect a cloverleaf skull
MRI of the brain and craniocervical junction for hydrocephalus and hindbrain herniation
Radiographs of the hands and feet to document broad thumbs, great toes and syndactyly
Airway endoscopy and polysomnography, especially in severe forms with tracheal anomalies
Ophthalmology review for proptosis and corneal protection
redFlags: Cloverleaf skull with extreme proptosis endangering the globes
Airway obstruction or a solid cartilaginous trachea causing respiratory failure
Rapidly progressive hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure
Symptomatic hindbrain herniation with brainstem compromise
reference.prognosis: Type 1 disease generally has a favourable outcome with normal cognition after craniofacial management, whereas types 2 and 3 carry high early morbidity and mortality from airway, brain and visual complications and demand intensive multidisciplinary care.
pitfalls: Assuming a good prognosis without determining the clinical subtype
Missing tracheal cartilage abnormalities as a cause of respiratory difficulty
Failing to protect severely proptotic globes
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Staged craniofacial surgery with early cranial vault expansion and suture release to relieve raised intracranial pressure, followed by later midface advancement for midface hypoplasia and proptosis
Airway protection in severe forms, managing upper-airway and tracheal cartilage anomalies, with tracheostomy where obstruction is life-threatening
Corneal protection for severe proptosis using lubrication and tarsorrhaphy to prevent exposure keratopathy and globe damage
Neurosurgical management of hydrocephalus by shunting and of hindbrain herniation by craniocervical decompression
Hand and foot surgery for broad, medially deviated thumbs and great toes and for soft-tissue syndactyly
Surveillance for raised intracranial pressure, hearing loss and obstructive sleep apnoea with serial cranial imaging and polysomnography
Clinical genetics referral with FGFR1 and FGFR2 testing and family counselling, within multidisciplinary craniofacial team care
